---
title: "Single-arm meta-analysis"
subtitle: "Pooling a proportion or a mean, with no comparison group"
---

Use this module when there is no comparison: you want the pooled prevalence of a
condition, the complication rate of a procedure, or the average value of a
measure in a population. Follow [the three-step flow](flow.qmd), with a much shorter step 2, because
without a control group several fields stop making sense.

## Step 1, the data

Two submodules, chosen on the previous page.

**Single proportions**

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `study` | the study label |
| `event` | number of participants with the outcome |
| `n` | sample size of the arm |

**Single means**

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `study` | the study label |
| `n` | sample size |
| `mean` | mean value of the outcome |
| `sd` | standard deviation of the outcome |

#### A study reporting a median is accepted too

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `study`, `n` | as above |
| `median`, `q1`, `q3` | median and quartiles of the outcome |

`min` and `max` are optional. They can stand in for the quartiles when a paper
reports only a range, and the conversion is then less precise.

A median with `sd` and nothing else is refused, and on purpose. A median cannot
be turned into a mean without the quartiles or the range, and `meta` does not
complain about it: it drops the study from the pooling with no message. Better
to hear it here than to publish a review missing studies you never knew were
excluded.

#### The two can be mixed in one file

Fill the columns each study reports and leave the rest empty. The example dataset
does exactly that: eight studies with mean and SD, four with median and
quartiles. MetaVidence converts the median studies before pooling, using the
method of Luo and colleagues for the mean and that of Shi and colleagues for the
standard deviation, which are the current defaults of the `meta` package.

The **Data check** reports how many studies were converted, so the number is in
front of you before anything runs and can go straight into the methods section.

Mean and SD remains the ideal input: it is what the study measured, with nothing
estimated. The conversion is there so that a study reporting a median can join
the analysis instead of being left out, not as an equivalent choice.

Extra columns stay available for subgroup analysis and meta-regression, as in
the other modules. The **Data check** verifies the required ones, counts the
studies and flags problems, including `event` larger than `n`.

## Step 2, the parameters

The outcome direction field and the group name fields do not exist here: with no
comparison, there is no "favors experimental" or "favors control" to label.

### Single proportions

**Outcome name** goes into titles and file names, as always.

**Summary measure (sm)** (default `PLOGIT`) chooses the transformation.
Proportions near 0% or 100% have too small a variance and distort the pooling if
used raw, which is why the transformation exists:

* `PLOGIT`, logit. The default, and the recommendation for most cases.
* `PFT`, Freeman-Tukey double arcsine. Stabilizes the variance when there are
  proportions very close to the extremes, but the way back to the percentage
  scale is problematic when sample sizes vary a lot between studies. Use it
  knowing that.
* `PAS`, plain arcsine.
* `PLN`, log of the proportion.
* `PRAW`, raw proportion, untransformed. Only sensible when every proportion is
  far from 0% and 100%.

Results always return to the percentage scale in plots and tables, so the
transformation is a choice of method, not of presentation.

**Method** (default `Inverse`) chooses between `Inverse`, inverse variance, and
`GLMM`, a random-intercept logistic model.

Recommendation: keep `Inverse`, which is what the large majority of published
prevalence meta-analyses use, and leave `Tau method` at `REML`.

Switch to `GLMM` with `Tau method` at `ML` when your dataset has:

* studies with zero events, or
* proportions very close to 0% or 100%.

In those two situations `Inverse` has to add 0.5 to each cell, a continuity
correction that shifts precisely the extreme studies, which are the ones you are
trying to estimate well. `GLMM` models the counts directly and needs no such
correction.

::: {.callout-note}
## GLMM has no weight column
A GLMM fit produces no per-study weight, so the forest plot comes out without
the Weight column and with every square the same size. This is not a defect of
the plot: the weight simply does not exist in that model. If the weight column
matters for the figure in your paper, that is an argument in favour of
`Inverse`.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## GLMM requires PLOGIT
If you switch `sm` to `PFT`, `PAS`, `PLN` or `PRAW` and leave the method at
`GLMM`, the analysis stops with an error message. When you change `sm`, set the
method back to `Inverse`.
:::

**Analysis model** and **Tau method** work as in the binary module.

This submodule has no **Prediction interval**, no **Random CI method** and no
**Prediction method**.

### Single means

**Summary measure (sm)** (default `MRAW`) has two options. `MRAW` pools the raw
mean, in the original unit, and is the recommendation. `MLN` pools the log of
the mean, useful when the measure is positive and strongly skewed, such as time
to an event or serum concentration.

**Analysis model**, **Tau method** (default `REML`) and **Prediction interval**
(default `Yes`) work as in the binary module. There is no **Method** field, no
**Random CI method** and no **Prediction method**.

## Step 3, export and results

Both submodules carry the same cards as the paired modules: **Forest plot**,
**Leave-one-out analysis**, **Funnel plot**, **Small-study effects** with
Egger's test, **Subgroup analysis**, **Meta-regression** and the two summary
tables as XLSX.
